title: The Cat Who Crossed the City
summary: Curiosity sends Michi into a big blue truck, and he wakes up on the far side of the city, a long way from the window where someone is always waiting.

scenes.text: Michi was a gray cat with four white paws, as if he had walked through flour. He lived with Lucía in a small house on Almond Tree Street, next door to a bakery that smelled of warm bread all morning long. Every afternoon Lucía came home from school and lifted him into her arms. "Did you wait for me all day?" she would ask, and the whole house filled up with her laugh. Michi purred and closed his eyes. That was his favorite place in the world. That Thursday, though, a blue truck stopped in front of the bakery. It carried boxes stacked up to the roof and smelled of new things, of faraway places. Along the sidewalk, the wind stirred the dry leaves. Michi felt a tickle at the tip of his tail: the tickle of curiosity. He looked at the truck's open door and at the biggest box. And without thinking too much, he jumped inside.

Inside the truck everything was shadowy and smelled of cardboard. Michi found a soft corner between two boxes, turned around three times and settled in like a little bread roll. Outside, hands were pushing the boxes. Michi heard a door slam and a few footsteps. The engine coughed, shivered, and the floor began to move. At first it was fun: the truck rocked like a cradle and through a crack came a thread of wind. It tickled his whiskers. Michi yawned. He closed one eye. He closed the other. And he fell asleep, dreaming of warm milk. When he woke up, the truck was still and the door was open. Michi poked out his nose, jumped down and looked around. There was no bakery. There were no almond trees. His house was not there. There were tall buildings, blinking traffic lights and people walking fast without looking down. Michi sat, his tail pressed tight against his body, and understood that he was far away. Very, very far.

The city made an enormous noise. Horns, brakes, a siren far away. Michi walked close to the walls, trying to make himself small, until a garbage can tipped over nearby with a dry thud. Michi jumped so high he almost touched a sign. That was when he heard them. Behind a fence, staring at him and barking with all their might, were two big dogs. Woof, woof! Michi squeezed under a car and stayed there, trembling, his heart going thump-thump-thump inside his ears. "I want to go home," he said quietly. "I want my blanket and my Lucía." He waited a long while. The two of them got tired of barking. The street grew calmer. Michi poked out one whisker first, then half a nose, then a paw. The air smelled of smoke and old rain, but it did not smell of danger anymore. He came out slowly and decided he would not stay crying under a car.

High on a lamppost sat a plump gray pigeon with eyes as bright as two seeds. She had watched him for a while. "You're lost, aren't you?" said the pigeon, fluttering down. "I can tell by your ears." "I live next to a bakery," answered Michi. "It smells of warm bread. There are almond trees on the sidewalk." "Ah, I know that neighborhood. I fly all over the city," she said, and brought her beak closer as if telling him a secret. Her voice turned into a whisper. "Always walk toward the place where the sun is going down. Cross the big park. Then the market. At the end you will see a bridge over the river: cross it without fear and you will be close. And when you don't know what to do, close your eyes and smell." Past the flowers of a balcony buzzed a bee. Michi looked at the orange sun and said, "Thank you, pigeon. I will make it."

The big park appeared around a corner, green and enormous, as if somebody had tucked a piece of the countryside inside the city. Michi slipped in under a bench and felt the cool grass on his belly. Out there the noise of the cars stayed outside. He could hear birds, a ball, the squeak of a swing. He walked beside a pond where the last of the sunlight lit up the water. On a stone sat a frog. It went croak, croak, as if saying hello. Michi answered with a short meow and went on. Two children wanted to pet him and he let them for a moment, because their hands felt like Lucía's hands. But when the smaller one tried to hug him, Michi slipped away gently. He could not stay: he had a home waiting for him. On the other side of the park, between the trees, the sun was already hiding. Michi walked faster.

The market was a tunnel of smells. Oranges, cilantro, fish, fresh bread, wet flowers. Michi walked between baskets and table legs, dodging hurried shoes. Someone was sweeping. Someone was closing a metal shutter. A cart rolled by and sprinkled his tail as it splashed through a puddle. An orange cat, very skinny, spotted him from the top of some boxes and meowed. He wanted to know who this stranger was. "I'm on my way back home," Michi explained. "Good luck, then," said the other cat, and moved aside. Just then Michi smelled something wonderful: fish. A lady in a blue apron, the one at the very last stall, crouched down and left him a piece on a scrap of paper. "Eat, little one," she said. "You're a long way from home, aren't you?" Michi ate it all and licked his whiskers. For the first time all day his tummy was happy. And night was beginning to fall over the city.

The bridge appeared at the end of a long street, with two rows of lamps lit like candles. Down below, the river murmured patiently, talking to itself. Michi stopped at the entrance. The bridge was very long and he was very small. High above everything, white and round as if freshly washed, shone the moon. From a tree on the bank hooted an owl. Hoo, hoooo. Michi swallowed hard. "No fear," he told himself, just as the pigeon had said. "One step, and another step." And he began to cross. His white paws crossed the planks step by step: tap, tap, tap. The river wind combed his fur backward and carried the smell of deep water. Halfway across he stopped to look at the city lights reflected below, trembling like golden fish. It was beautiful. Michi took a deep breath, wiggled his ears and kept going to the other side.

On the other side of the river the streets were narrower and quieter. Michi walked beneath the cables, and between them peeked a few stars. Suddenly he stopped with one paw in the air. He closed his eyes, the way the pigeon had taught him. And he smelled. Bread. Warm bread. That bread. It was a thin, thin thread of smell coming from the corner. Michi followed it with his nose in the air and, three blocks later, he saw something he knew: a crooked tree, a green fence, a small puddle where he always stopped to drink. The almond trees! His street! Then he ran. Never in his life had he run like that, ears back, jumping the edge of the sidewalk, dodging a bicycle, his tail up like a flag. He passed the closed bakery, passed the same old lamppost and braked in front of a door painted yellow. He scratched the wood and meowed loudly, very loudly.

Inside, feet came running, a chair moved, and there was Lucía's voice saying, "Mom, it's him, it's him!" Then somebody threw open the door. And there she stood, in her pajamas, with messy hair and enormous eyes. "Michi!" she shouted. "You came back!" A sob got mixed up with her laugh. She lifted him into her arms and squeezed him so tightly that Michi had to wriggle. She kissed his head and told him everything at once: that she had put up posters on the lampposts, that she had left a plate on the windowsill every single night, that she had not wanted dessert even once. Michi purred so hard that his whole body hummed. Lucía's mom brought warm milk and checked his paws. "He's all in one piece," she said. "Skinny and very dirty, but all in one piece." Outside, the huge city kept making noise. Inside, everything was back in its place.

Then came the shortest bath in history, a towel that smelled of clean, and a soft brushing. Lucía carried him to her room and put him in the usual spot: at the foot of the bed, on the checkered blanket. She turned off the big light and left the corner lamp on. "Tomorrow I'll tell you everything that happened at school," she said quietly. "But now we sleep." Michi kneaded the blanket with his white paws, curled into a round ball and breathed. Three deep breaths, as if he were keeping the whole city in his chest and then letting it go. Cool air came in through the window, along with the calm song of the crickets. There were no more trucks, no fences, no bridges. Only Lucía's hand on his back, going up and down, slowly. And then, from deep inside the chest of a happy cat, came a small snore. Michi fell fast asleep.
